mainTopic: When טבל becomes fixed for מעשר (בית or חצר), and how this fits the ברייתא about the owner, the worker and the buyer
overview: This amud asks when untithed produce (טבל) becomes 'fixed,' so that even a snack needs מעשר first. רבי ינאי says this happens only once the produce 'sees the front of the house,' based on 'בערתי הקדש מן הבית.' רבי יוחנן says even a חצר is enough, based on 'ואכלו בשעריך ושבעו.' Each side explains the other's פסוק. For רבי יוחנן, 'house' teaches that the חצר must be guarded like a house. For רבי ינאי, 'your gates' teaches that the produce must come in through the gate, not over rooftops or through enclosures. רב חנינא חוזאה then challenges both views from a ברייתא. It says the owner and the worker may eat without מעשר, which implies that a buyer is obligated even in the field. רב פפא answers that the case is a fig tree whose branches lean into a חצר or a בית. The owner is still exempt because he focuses on his tree, which stands outside, while the buyer focuses on the fruit he bought. Finally the גמרא asks whether a buyer is obligated by Torah law at all, and begins quoting a ברייתא about the shops of בית הינו. That ברייתא continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי ינאי: produce is obligated only once it sees the front of the house
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי's statement ends here: טבל becomes obligated in מעשר only when it is brought in through the front of the house. His source is 'I have removed the holy from the house.'
steps.simpleTranslation: [Untithed produce is not obligated in tithes] until it sees the front of the house, as it says: 'I have removed the holy from the house.'
steps.whatsHappening: We are finishing רבי ינאי's rule. Produce only becomes 'fixed' for מעשר when it is brought into the house through its front entrance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק from וידוי מעשרות speaks of removing the holy portions 'from the house.' רבי ינאי reads this to mean that the house is what triggers the obligation to separate מעשר. Before the produce enters the house, one may still eat from it casually without tithing.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce from which תרומות and מעשרות have not yet been separated
The front of the house, its main entrance
'I have removed the holy': words from the declaration said when tithes are given out
Tithe, the tenth portion of produce that must be separated

steps.confusionAlert: This rule is about when produce becomes 'fixed' so that even a casual snack requires tithing first. It is not about whether the produce needs מעשר at all. All produce eventually needs it.

phrases.english: until it sees the front of the house,
phrases.notes: This finishes רבי ינאי's line from just before: untithed produce isn't obligated in מעשר until this point.

phrases.english: as it is stated: “I have removed the holy from the house.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי ינאי's statement, which began before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טבל becomes obligated in מעשר only once it enters through the front of the house

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: even a courtyard fixes the obligation
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן argues that bringing produce into a חצר is already enough to obligate it in מעשר. His source is 'and they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Even a courtyard fixes [the produce for tithes], as it says: 'and they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the opposing view. You don't need a house; a חצר is enough to make the produce obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Your gates' points to the area just inside the entrance, which is the courtyard. So according to רבי יוחנן, the obligation starts earlier than רבי ינאי said, at the חצר and not only at the house.

keyTerms.meaning: Courtyard, the enclosed yard in front of a house
Fixes, meaning it makes the produce obligated in tithes
'In your gates', in the area inside your entrance

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Even a courtyard fixes [the obligation],
as it is stated: “And they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ חָצֵר קוֹבַעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי ינאי and offers a different פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bringing produce into a חצר already obligates it in מעשר

steps.title: Challenge to רבי יוחנן: the verse says 'from the house'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks רבי יוחנן how he deals with רבי ינאי's פסוק, which clearly says 'from the house.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבי יוחנן too, isn't it written 'from the house'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן. The תורה says 'house,' so how can a courtyard be enough?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each side has a פסוק, so each side must explain the other's פסוק. Here the גמרא asks what רבי יוחנן does with the word 'הבית.'

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written: a phrase that throws a פסוק back at someone
Also, too

phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Yochanan too,
isn't it written “from the house”!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן using רבי ינאי's פסוק
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that a חצר is enough
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק explicitly mentions a house, which suggests a courtyard is not enough

steps.title: Answer: the courtyard must be guarded like a house
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads 'house' as a model. A חצר counts only if it is secured and private, the way a house is.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would tell you: a courtyard is like a house. Just as a house is guarded, so too the courtyard must be guarded.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי יוחנן. The word 'house' doesn't exclude a courtyard; it tells us what kind of courtyard counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן keeps both פסוקים. 'Your gates' teaches that a חצר works, and 'house' teaches that it must be a guarded one. A courtyard open to the public would not fix the produce.

keyTerms.meaning: He would say to you: the גמרא answering on someone's behalf
Similar to, like
That is guarded or secured
Just as ... so too: a comparison formula

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, a חצר fixes produce for מעשר, but only a guarded, private חצר that is 'like a house.'

phrases.english: He would say to you:
a courtyard is similar to a house:
just as a house is guarded,
so too a courtyard that is guarded.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבי יוחנן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the פסוק: 'house' defines the quality of the courtyard instead of excluding it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'From the house' seemed to require an actual house
steps.terutzMaskana: 'House' teaches that the courtyard must be guarded like a house

steps.title: Challenge to רבי ינאי: the verse says 'in your gates'
steps.stepSummary: Now the גמרא turns to רבי ינאי and asks what he does with רבי יוחנן's פסוק, 'in your gates.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי ינאי too, isn't it written 'in your gates'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי ינאי the same way. The פסוק says 'gates,' which sounds like a courtyard, so why does he require a house?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors step 3. If 'בשעריך' points to the courtyard, רבי ינאי must explain why that word doesn't make a courtyard enough.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written: a short form of הָא כְּתִיב

phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Yannai too,
isn't it written “in your gates”!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel challenge, now aimed at רבי ינאי
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's ruling that only the house fixes produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק mentions 'gates,' which suggests the courtyard area is enough

steps.title: Answer: produce must come in through the gate, not over roofs
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי uses 'your gates' for a different teaching. The produce must be brought in through the proper entrance. Produce brought in over rooftops or through enclosures is not fixed for מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: That [פסוק] is needed to teach that one brings it in through the gate. This excludes bringing it in through rooftops and enclosures, which does not [fix it].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי ינאי. 'Gates' is not about the courtyard; it teaches how the produce must enter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי ינאי, the house is still what fixes the produce. But it must be brought in the normal way, through the entrance. If it is brought in over rooftops or through enclosures, it is not considered to have 'seen the front of the house,' so it is not fixed.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it [for something else]: the פסוק is used for another teaching
To exclude
Rooftops
Enclosures: fenced areas, usually outside the town, not used for living

steps.whatToRemember: Both אמוראים use both פסוקים. רבי יוחנן: a חצר fixes produce if it is guarded like a house. רבי ינאי: only the house fixes it, and only when the produce comes in through the gate.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the obligation depends on how the produce arrives, not just where it ends up. Bringing it in an unusual way can keep it from becoming fixed for מעשר.

phrases.english: That [verse] he needs
[to teach] that one brings it in by way of the gate,
to exclude [bringing it] by way of rooftops and enclosures, which does not [fix it].

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ דִּמְעַיֵּיל לֵיהּ דֶּרֶךְ שַׁעַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבי ינאי
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirecting the פסוק to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'In your gates' seemed to make the courtyard enough
steps.terutzMaskana: 'In your gates' teaches that produce must enter through the gate, excluding rooftops and enclosures

steps.title: רב חנינא חוזאה quotes a ברייתא about the worker eating
steps.stepSummary: רב חנינא חוזאה opens an objection by quoting a ברייתא. It reads 'כנפשך' as comparing the פועל to the owner: both may eat and are פטור from מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנינא חוזאה objects: 'Like yourself' means the worker is like you. Just as you, the owner, eat and are exempt, so too the worker eats and is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge. רב חנינא חוזאה quotes a ברייתא, and the actual question comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word כנפשך ('like yourself') is read as 'the worker is like you, the owner.' The owner may eat a casual snack from his own produce without separating מעשר. So the פועל may do the same. This sets up an inference about someone who is not the owner or a worker.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection, usually from a ברייתא or משנה
'Like yourself' (from the פסוק about a worker eating grapes)
A hired worker in the field
Exempt (here: exempt from separating מעשר)

phrases.english: Rav Ḥanina Ḥoza'a raises an objection:
"Like yourself" – so is the worker himself,
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25. The ברייתא reads 'like yourself' as 'the worker is like you, the owner.'

phrases.english: just as you yourself eat and are exempt,

phrases.aramaic: אַף נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל פּוֹעֵל אוֹכֵל וּפָטוּר.
phrases.english: so too the worker himself eats and is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the two פסוקים have been settled, a new objection is raised from a ברייתא that affects both רבי יוחנן and רבי ינאי.
steps.kashyaTarget: Both רבי יוחנן (חצר) and רבי ינאי (בית)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source is quoted here. The attack itself comes in the next step, through an inference about a buyer.

steps.title: A buyer is obligated, even in the field?
steps.stepSummary: From the ברייתא we can infer that a buyer is obligated in מעשר. That seems to apply even in the field, before the produce enters any חצר or בית.
steps.simpleTranslation: This implies that a buyer is obligated. Isn't that talking about produce still in the field?
steps.whatsHappening: Here is the actual challenge. If only the owner and the worker are exempt, a buyer must be obligated, and that seems true even out in the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both רבי יוחנן and רבי ינאי say produce becomes obligated only once it enters a חצר or a בית. But this ברייתא seems to obligate a buyer right there in the field. If so, entering a חצר or בית would not be needed, which goes against both opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: A buyer of produce
Obligated (here: in מעשר)
'Isn't it...?' A way of pushing an inference

phrases.english: This implies a buyer is obligated,
isn't it talking about one in the field?
phrases.notes: Meaning the fruit never entered a courtyard or house, so why would the buyer be obligated?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא לוֹקֵחַ חַיָּיב, מַאי לָאו בַּשָּׂדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenging inference from the ברייתא quoted in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of both רבי יוחנן and רבי ינאי that entering a חצר or בית is needed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A buyer is obligated even in the field. So a buyer becomes obligated without the produce entering a חצר or בית.

steps.title: רב פפא: a fig tree whose branches lean into the חצר
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the ברייתא is talking about a fig tree in a garden whose branches lean into a חצר. For the view that requires a בית, the branches lean into a house.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Here we are dealing with a fig tree standing in a garden whose branches lean into a courtyard. For the one who says 'house,' they lean into a house.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge. The buyer in the ברייתא is not really 'in the field,' because the fruit is hanging inside the חצר or בית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tree grows outside, but the fruit hangs over into the protected space. For רבי יוחנן that space is a חצר, and for רבי ינאי it is a בית. So the buyer's obligation still fits the rule that produce must be in a חצר or בית, and both opinions survive.

keyTerms.meaning: A fig tree
A garden (outside the courtyard)
Its branches and leaves (its top)
We are dealing with

steps.confusionAlert: רב פפא is not saying the buyer is obligated out in the field. The fruit is physically hanging inside the חצר or בית, even though the tree's trunk is outside.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Here, with a fig tree standing in a garden
whose branches lean into a courtyard, we are dealing,
and for the one who says 'into a house', into a house.
phrases.notes: That's רבי ינאי, who needs the fruit to reach the house, not just the courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא הָכָא בִּתְאֵנָה הָעוֹמֶדֶת בְּגִינָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's buyer is obligated while the produce is in the open field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fruit hangs into a חצר (for רבי יוחנן) or a בית (for רבי ינאי), so the normal requirement is met.

steps.title: Then the owner should be obligated too
steps.stepSummary: If the fruit is inside the חצר or בית, the owner should also be obligated. Yet the ברייתא says he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the homeowner should also be obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב פפא. If the fruit counts as being inside, why is the owner still allowed to eat without מעשר?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא's case puts the fruit in the protected space. That should obligate anyone who eats it, including the owner. But the ברייתא clearly says the owner is פטור, so the answer seems to create a new problem.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introduces a problem with the last answer)
The owner (homeowner)
Should be obligated

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי בַּעַל הַבַּיִת נָמֵי נִיחַיַּיב!
phrases.english: If so, the homeowner should also be obligated!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי בַּעַל הַבַּיִת נָמֵי נִיחַיַּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's answer from step 9 using the owner's exemption in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's case of the fig tree leaning into the חצר or בית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the location obligates the buyer, it should obligate the owner too. Yet the ברייתא exempts him.

steps.title: Owner looks at his tree, buyer looks at his purchase
steps.stepSummary: The owner thinks of the tree as a whole, and the tree stands outside. The buyer thinks of the fruit he bought, and the fruit is inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: The homeowner's eyes are on his fig tree, and the buyer's eyes are on his purchase.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the owner is still פטור. It depends on what each person is focused on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the owner, what matters is the tree, and the main part of the tree is in the garden outside. For the buyer, what matters is only the fruit he bought, and that fruit is hanging inside the חצר or בית. So the same fruit obligates the buyer but not the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: His eyes (his focus or attention)
His purchase

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא fits both רבי יוחנן and רבי ינאי. It is talking about fruit hanging into a חצר or בית. The buyer, who focuses on the fruit, is obligated. The owner, who focuses on his tree outside, is not.

phrases.english: The homeowner's eyes are on his fig tree,
phrases.notes: He thinks about the whole tree, and most of it stands outside in the garden.

phrases.english: and the buyer's eyes are on his purchase.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת עֵינָיו בִּתְאֵנָתוֹ וְלוֹקֵחַ עֵינָיו בְּמִקָּחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 and defends רב פפא's answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fruit inside the חצר or בית should obligate everyone equally.
steps.terutzMaskana: What counts is each person's focus. The owner focuses on the tree, which stands outside. The buyer focuses on the fruit, which hangs inside.

steps.title: Is a buyer really obligated by Torah law?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether a לוקח is obligated in מעשר מדאורייתא at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is a buyer obligated by Torah law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge to the ברייתא from Step 7. It asks whether a person who buys produce is really obligated in מעשר by Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learned its rules from the Torah word כנפשך. So when we inferred from it that a buyer is obligated (Step 8), that sounded like a Torah-level obligation. The גמרא now doubts that a buyer's obligation comes from the Torah at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A buyer, here someone who bought produce
By Torah law, as opposed to a rabbinic rule
Is he obligated? (a doubting question)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not asking whether a buyer must separate מעשר at all. It is only asking whether the obligation comes from the Torah or from the Rabbis.

phrases.english: And is a buyer obligated by Torah law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts רב פפא's setting from Steps 9 and 11, then attacks the deeper assumption that a buyer's obligation is a Torah-level obligation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference from the כנפשך ברייתא that a buyer is obligated in מעשר by Torah law
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a buyer is not obligated by Torah law, then a ברייתא built on a Torah verse should not be making him obligated.

steps.title: The shops of בית הינו were destroyed for relying only on Torah law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא: the shops of בית הינו were destroyed three years before ירושלים because their people followed only the strict Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: Why were the shops of בית הינו destroyed three years before ירושלים? Because they based their practice on the words of the Torah alone. For they would say:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as the source for its challenge. This line sets up the next move: the ברייתא is about to quote what the people of בית הינו used to say.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says these shops were punished for keeping only the strict letter of Torah law. That means the Rabbis required more than the Torah did in their kind of case. Their exact words, which come on the next amud, will show how this connects to buying produce and מעשר.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught in a ברייתא (introduces a source used to challenge)
Shops or stores
A place near ירושלים known for its shops
They based their practice only on the strict Torah law

phrases.english: But it was taught: For what reason were destroyed
the shops of בית הינו
three years before ירושלים?
phrases.notes: He means three years before ירושלים itself was destroyed.

phrases.english: Because they based their practices
on the words of the Torah.
phrases.notes: The point is that they kept only what the Torah itself required and ignored the extra rules of the Rabbis.

phrases.english: For they would say:
phrases.notes: The sentence stops here. What they used to say comes on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא מִפְּנֵי מָה חָרְבוּ חֲנוּיוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית הִינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the question in Step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That a buyer is not obligated in מעשר by Torah law
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about the shops of בית הינו, which were destroyed for relying only on strict Torah law
